# Project Charter

<!-- Generated by `spec-kitty charter generate` -->

Generated: 2026-08-14T19:45:49Z

## Testing Standards

- Test-driven development is required. Start each observable behavior with a failing acceptance, contract, integration, or unit test at the narrowest stable entry point. Use deterministic fixtures for DSH boot, stream, RPC, reconnect, upgrade, and plugin behavior; exercise packaged applications and real process boundaries for release-critical flows. Changed executable source must have complete branch coverage unless a documented platform-only path is covered in its platform CI job.

## Quality Gates

- Type checking, linting, formatting, focused tests, dependency and license audits, packaging smoke tests, and compatibility checks must pass before merge. A release candidate must load every first-party Web contribution and at least one out-of-tree dynamic client plugin without modification, expose no unauthenticated TCP listener, recover from renderer and Host failure, and preserve sessions and settings across an atomic upgrade. No patch-package or vendored edits to upstream DSH are permitted.

## Performance Benchmarks

- Memory is the highest-priority performance dimension, followed by long-session and streaming responsiveness, then startup. Measure the complete application process tree on a declared reference Mac with identical payloads and fixtures. During sustained streams, input-to-next-paint must be at most 50 ms at p95 and below 100 ms at p99, with no main-loop stall of 250 ms or longer. Warm launch must be prompt-ready within 1.5 seconds at p95 and cold launch within 3 seconds at p95. Retained state must grow linearly only with the configured active history window and be reclaimable after session switching. Tauri becomes the production shell only if all parity gates pass and its complete-process-tree memory is at least 25 percent lower than Electron across the representative p95 scenarios without a material responsiveness or startup regression.

## Branch Strategy

- Changes land through focused pull requests from codex/* or feat/* branches to main using conventional commits. At least one independent review is required for production changes; security, updater, signing, IPC, process lifecycle, and compatibility changes require an explicit threat or failure-mode review. Generated mission status artifacts are not hand-edited.
- Deployment constraints: Ship macOS arm64 first as a signed, hardened, notarized direct-download application, then macOS x64 and signed Windows packages, with Linux after the platform WebView and packaging matrix passes. Do not target the Mac App Store initially because arbitrary workspaces, subprocesses, terminals, and dynamic plugins are core capabilities. Bundle an exact supported Node runtime and an exact DSH release; update the shell, runtime, adapter, and DSH payload atomically. Update signatures are mandatory and rollback or recovery must not corrupt the user's DSH home.

## Policy Summary

- Intent: Build and independently release the most capable DeepSeek Harness desktop client, with macOS first and Windows and Linux following. The product must preserve the official DSH Web experience, first-party capabilities, and third-party client plugins while adding native desktop lifecycle, security, packaging, updates, and system integration. It must consume upstream as a versioned dependency rather than fork or patch it, so upstream upgrades are normally an automated version bump plus small adapter changes.
- Languages/Frameworks: Use TypeScript and Node.js for the shared payload, compatibility adapter, supervisor, tests, and tooling. Evaluate Tauri 2 with Rust against an Electron reference shell using the exact same official renderer and standard Node sidecar. The selected production shell must be decided by measured parity, whole-process-tree memory, responsiveness, and startup results rather than framework reputation. Keep packages ESM-first and cross-platform.
- Testing: Test-driven development is required. Start each observable behavior with a failing acceptance, contract, integration, or unit test at the narrowest stable entry point. Use deterministic fixtures for DSH boot, stream, RPC, reconnect, upgrade, and plugin behavior; exercise packaged applications and real process boundaries for release-critical flows. No patch-package or vendored edits to upstream DSH are permitted.

At least one independent review is required for production changes; security, updater, signing, IPC, process lifecycle, and compatibility changes require an explicit threat or failure-mode review. Generated mission status artifacts are not hand-edited.

Retained state must grow linearly only with the configured active history window and be reclaimable after session switching. Tauri becomes the production shell only if all parity gates pass and its complete-process-tree memory is at least 25 percent lower than Electron across the representative p95 scenarios without a material responsiveness or startup regression.

## Project Directives

1. Specification Fidelity Requirement (`DIRECTIVE_010`): Implemented behavior and produced artifacts must remain faithful to approved specifications, with any necessary deviations explicitly documented and reviewed before acceptance.
   - Scope: Applies to planning outputs, work-package implementation, and review checks where spec drift can silently change product behavior.
   - Procedure: Trace each implementation change to explicit requirements or acceptance criteria.
   - Procedure: Flag and document deviations before merge when the spec must evolve.
   - Procedure: Validate that final behavior matches committed scope and constraints.
   - Integrity rule: Unrecorded scope drift is not permitted.
   - Integrity rule: Requirement-to-implementation traceability must remain inspectable.
   - Validation criterion: Review notes identify how changed behavior maps to specification language.
   - Validation criterion: Any deliberate spec deviation has linked rationale and approval context.
2. Locality of Change (`DIRECTIVE_024`): Changes should stay close to the problem being solved to reduce blast radius, simplify review, and lower regression risk.
   - Scope: Applies to code, tests, and documentation modifications made while executing a defined work package or bug fix.
   - Procedure: Limit edits to files and modules directly related to the target behavior.
   - Procedure: Separate opportunistic cleanup from functional work unless it is required for correctness.
   - Procedure: Review diffs for scope creep before committing.
   - Integrity rule: Unrelated refactors must not be mixed into scoped implementation tasks.
   - Integrity rule: Cross-cutting changes require explicit rationale and approval context.
   - Validation criterion: Reviewers can map each changed file to the stated task objective.
   - Validation criterion: Diffs avoid unrelated churn that increases review complexity.
3. Test and Typecheck Quality Gate (`DIRECTIVE_030`): Code changes must pass the relevant automated tests and static validation gates before handoff so regressions and interface drift are caught early.
   - Scope: Applies to source code, tests, and command workflows that change executable behavior or typed interfaces.
   - Procedure: Run unit tests for changed core logic and integration tests for changed workflow boundaries.
   - Procedure: Meet the repository coverage expectation for new code, or document the delta when pre-existing scope makes that impractical.
   - Procedure: Run the repository's applicable static analysis, typing, lint, or equivalent validation gates for the affected scope.
   - Procedure: Run configured or enabled CVE, dependency, or license-compliance checks when the repository treats them as part of the validation gate.
   - Procedure: Record any remaining pre-existing failures separately from newly introduced failures before handoff.
   - Integrity rule: New behavior is not ready for review while relevant tests or applicable static validation gates are red.
   - Integrity rule: Configured supply-chain or compliance gates must not be skipped silently when they are part of the repository's expected validation flow.
   - Integrity rule: Pre-existing validation debt must not be hidden inside new work.
   - Validation criterion: Relevant test suites pass for the changed scope before review handoff.
   - Validation criterion: New code meets the repository coverage target or any accepted shortfall is called out explicitly.
   - Validation criterion: Applicable static validation gates pass for the affected scope, or any pre-existing unrelated failures are identified explicitly.
   - Validation criterion: Applicable CVE, dependency, and license checks pass when those gates are configured for the affected scope, or any pre-existing unrelated failures are identified explicitly.
4. Test-First Development (`DIRECTIVE_034`): Require test-first behavior across acceptance and implementation layers, selecting tactics based on scope and risk. Tests define the contract before production code is written.
   - Scope: Applies to all implementation work that produces executable behavior — new features, bug fixes, and refactoring that changes observable output.
   - Procedure: Write a failing test that captures the intended behavior before writing production code.
   - Procedure: Select the appropriate test-first tactic based on scope — acceptance-test-first for feature boundaries, tdd-red-green-refactor for unit-level iteration, zombies-tdd for incremental case discovery.
   - Procedure: Keep the red-green-refactor cycle short — each cycle should take minutes, not hours.
   - Procedure: When fixing a bug, write a reproduction test first that fails, then apply the fix.
   - Procedure: Reproduce the bug through the PRE-EXISTING (stable) entry point — the command, public function, or seam that exists on the unfixed code — never through the fix's not-yet-written API. A reproduction test must go red BECAUSE THE BUG MANIFESTS in the assertion (the wrong value/status/path/state), not because a new symbol or parameter the fix introduces is missing (ImportError/TypeError at collection).
   - Procedure: Prove red-first — run the reproduction test against the unfixed code and confirm it fails for the right reason, then apply the fix and confirm green. New-API unit tests are fine as contract coverage, but they are not the bug-capture.
   - Integrity rule: Production code must not be written ahead of a failing test that motivates it.
   - Integrity rule: Skipping the test-first cycle requires explicit justification in the commit or PR.
   - Integrity rule: A bug-reproduction test that can only run AFTER the fix exists (it imports the fix's new symbol or passes its new parameter) captures the fix's shape, not the bug — it is invalid; rewrite it to drive the stable entry point, and move any new-API import to lazy/in-test scope so the reproduction still collects and fails red on the unfixed code.
   - Validation criterion: Each new behavior has a corresponding test that was written before the production code.
   - Validation criterion: Bug fixes include a regression test that fails without the fix — and that failure is the bug's observable symptom (verified by running against the unfixed code), not a missing-new-symbol collection error.
5. Black-Box Integration Testing (`DIRECTIVE_036`): Exercise the system under test through its external interfaces only, without reference to its internal code structure, implementation details, or internal paths. Test cases derive from specifications, requirements, and design parameters, and assertions are made on observable outputs returned through those external interfaces. "Black-box" refers to the technique (absence of structural knowledge) and is independent of test scope — the scope is selected separately by responsibility, not by default to end-to-end.
   - Scope: Applies to integration-level tests — tests that exercise more than one collaborator together through an external interface of the system under test. The system under test may be a deployed service, a compose stack, or an in-process composition of a module and its collaborators; the responsibility boundary — not the deployment topology — determines what is inside the system under test for a given test. Unit-level tests and full end-to-end tests are governed by their own directives.
   - Procedure: Select the responsibility boundary for the test using the test-boundaries-by-responsibility tactic before writing the test.
   - Procedure: Derive test cases from specifications, requirements, and design parameters rather than from reading the implementation.
   - Procedure: Drive the system under test exclusively through its published external interface (e.g., HTTP request, CLI invocation, message send, public module API).
   - Procedure: Select both valid and invalid inputs and determine the expected output in advance of execution.
   - Procedure: Assert on observable outputs returned across the external interface — responses, status codes, persisted records, emitted events, logs, stored artifacts.
   - Procedure: Apply standard black-box design techniques where relevant — equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing, state transition testing, error guessing — to choose inputs.
   - Integrity rule: Black-box integration tests must not import inside-boundary modules of the system under test to invoke business logic directly.
   - Integrity rule: Black-box integration tests must not patch, monkeypatch, or otherwise replace inside-boundary collaborators of the system under test.
   - Integrity rule: Substitution of outside-boundary dependencies — other services, third-party systems, filesystem, network, clock — is permitted when the substitute preserves the observable contract the system under test relies on.
   - Integrity rule: Assertions must target externally observable state, not private attributes or internal call sequences of inside-boundary components.
   - Integrity rule: The responsibility boundary used by the test must be stated (in test name, docstring, or supporting doc) so reviewers can judge which components were exercised for real and which were substituted.
   - Validation criterion: Each black-box integration test can be read and understood without reference to the internal code structure of inside-boundary components.
   - Validation criterion: Each black-box integration test exercises the system under test through an external interface and asserts on observable outputs of that interface.
   - Validation criterion: Inputs for each test trace back to a specification, requirement, or design parameter rather than to an implementation detail.
   - Validation criterion: The responsibility boundary applied by the test is identifiable from the test itself.
6. Living Documentation Sync (`DIRECTIVE_037`): Behavior-describing artifacts must evolve together. When observable behavior changes, the canonical examples, acceptance checks, narrative specifications, user documentation, glossary terms, code-level documentation, and architecture records must be updated in the same change so no reader is left with a stale picture of the system.
   - Scope: Applies to specification, implementation, review, and documentation work that defines or changes externally observable behavior or the language used to describe it.
   - Procedure: Establish a small set of business-readable examples before planning implementation for new behavior.
   - Procedure: Promote stable examples into executable acceptance checks or document why automation is not yet feasible.
   - Procedure: Update example narratives, acceptance checks, spec references, user-facing docs, code-level docs, architecture notes, and glossary entries in the same change when behavior or domain language evolves.
   - Procedure: Remove or mark stale examples, doc passages, and glossary terms once they no longer describe supported behavior.
   - Integrity rule: Canonical examples must stay readable by domain stakeholders and must not depend on internal implementation detail.
   - Integrity rule: Behavior-changing work must not leave example, acceptance, spec, user-doc, code-doc, architecture, or glossary assets in disagreement.
   - Integrity rule: Example-to-requirement traceability must remain inspectable during review.
   - Integrity rule: Domain terms introduced or redefined by a change must be reflected in the glossary before the change is accepted.
   - Validation criterion: New or changed behavior is represented by at least one concrete example or an explicit no-example rationale approved in review.
   - Validation criterion: Acceptance checks or recorded manual verification map back to the updated canonical examples.
   - Validation criterion: Review evidence shows examples, specs, user docs, code-level docs, architecture records, and glossary entries remain aligned with observed behavior.
7. Canonical Sources and Unification (`DIRECTIVE_044`): Agents and operators must use the canonical doctrine template, skill, or CLI command rather than improvising a substitute or copying from a prior mission artifact, because older artifacts drift from the canonical surface and copying them propagates the drift. When a concept is found to live in more than one location (a split-brain surface), the correct response is to consolidate to a single canonical authority — not to add the same behavior to every copy. A documented CLI command that is absent from the running tool is a gap to file upstream, not an invitation to hand-roll a workaround.
   - Scope: Applies whenever an agent or operator selects a template, skill, or command to accomplish a task; whenever a split-brain surface is discovered during planning or implementation; and whenever a CLI command documented in canonical sources is found to be absent from the running tool.
   - Procedure: Rule 1 — Use canonical sources: always use the canonical template, skill, or CLI command surface rather than copying from a prior mission in kitty-specs/ or constructing an ad-hoc substitute. Templates under src/doctrine/missions/<type>/templates/ are the single source of truth, resolved through the charter/doctrine chain. Prior missions are historical snapshots — they drift and must never be used as copy sources.
   - Procedure: Rule 2 — Unification not parity: when a split-brain surface is found — the same concept implemented or stored in more than one location — consolidate to one canonical surface authority. Do NOT add the same behavior to every copy (parity); parity preserves the split-brain. Exception: do not drop a load-bearing invariant without a migration path proven safe by tests.
   - Procedure: Rule 3 — Missing command is a gap: when a CLI command is documented in canonical sources but absent from the running tool, trace its source and file an upstream gap issue. Do not silently hand-roll a substitute. The gap record and escalation to the team are the correct outputs, not a workaround committed to the codebase.
   - Integrity rule: No agent may copy a spec, plan, or tasks artifact from kitty-specs/ and use it as a template for a new mission; the canonical templates are the only valid starting points.
   - Integrity rule: Consolidating to a single canonical surface is the only acceptable resolution for a split-brain surface; adding parity to non-canonical copies is a red-line violation.
   - Integrity rule: A missing CLI command that is documented must produce a gap report and upstream issue, not a hand-rolled workaround committed to the codebase.
   - Validation criterion: New missions reference templates resolved through the charter/doctrine chain, not copied from prior missions in kitty-specs/.
   - Validation criterion: When a split-brain surface is remediated, one canonical route is established and non-canonical copies are retired or redirected — never augmented in parallel.
   - Validation criterion: Any hand-rolled substitute for a documented but absent CLI command is flagged as a violation and replaced with either the correct CLI invocation or a filed gap.
8. Respect risk boundaries: Never commit, log, transmit, or bundle user credentials or session contents in diagnostics. The renderer is sandboxed and receives only a narrow, versioned, capability-based bridge; arbitrary navigation, shell command construction, and unrestricted filesystem access are forbidden. The DSH Host runs in a standard Node sidecar for native-addon compatibility and must be terminated by exact process identity, never a broad process-name kill. Production data paths use private inherited IPC or an equivalently authenticated local transport and must not expose an unauthenticated loopback service. Unknown upstream versions fail with an actionable compatibility error instead of silently degrading.
9. Keep documentation synchronized with workflow and behavior changes: Keep architecture decisions, the upstream compatibility matrix, security model, performance methodology and results, release procedure, contributor setup, and user-facing limitations current in the same pull request as the behavior they describe. Specifications explain outcomes; implementation plans own technology choices; generated evidence links back to stable requirement identifiers.

This yields a reviewable pull-request-sized history, conflict-once rebases, and slice-granular bisection without risking silently dropped intent.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-clean-linear-commit-history.md` |
| `TACTIC:code-review-incremental` | tactic | Review a change set to identify correctness, structural, and architectural risks without rewriting or expanding scope. Formulate feedback as observations and questions, not instructions. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-code-review-incremental.md` |
| `TACTIC:connascence-analysis` | tactic | Diagnose coupling between software components by classifying it using the connascence taxonomy — examining strength, degree, and locality — and recommend targeted reductions that improve maintainability without unnecessary abstraction.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-connascence-analysis.md` |
| `TACTIC:context-mapping-classification` | tactic | Systematically classify every relationship between bounded contexts using the nine canonical DDD context mapping patterns and three relationship types. Produces an explicit map that reveals coupling, power asymmetries, and integration risk across the system. Based on Eric Evans's strategic design patterns and the DDD Crew context-mapping notation.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-context-mapping-classification.md` |
| `TACTIC:delete-the-assertion-not-the-test` | tactic | Remediate a friction test (one that passes for the wrong reason, false-reds a correct change, or asserts an implementation detail) by replacing its wrong assertion with a contract-pinned, red-first one while PRESERVING the test's setup and excavated edge-cases. Reserve outright deletion for tests that provably carry no unique coverage. This discharges "never delete a test to fix it" rigorously: never delete COVERAGE to dodge a failure. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-delete-the-assertion-not-the-test.md` |
| `TACTIC:domain-event-capture` | tactic | Funnel significant state changes through immutable Domain Event objects that are persisted before processing. Separates input recording from business reaction, enabling auditability, replay, and decoupled system evolution. Based on Martin Fowler's Domain Event pattern and Eric Evans's DDD events.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-domain-event-capture.md` |
| `TACTIC:eisenhower-prioritisation` | tactic | Assign each pending task an importance and urgency rating so that the most valuable work is tackled first and low-value work is explicitly eliminated or delegated. Prevents constant busyness from masking a lack of meaningful progress.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-eisenhower-prioritisation.md` |
| `TACTIC:five-paradigm-parallel-debugging` | tactic | Investigate stubborn, recurring, or shape-shifting bugs by dispatching five sub-agents in parallel, each constrained to a different debugging epistemology. Independent investigations converge on a single structural fix while each surfaces findings the others structurally cannot. Produces one structural intervention, not five point-fixes.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-five-paradigm-parallel-debugging.md` |
| `TACTIC:forensic-repository-audit` | tactic | Extract durable, evidence-backed signals about the health of an unfamiliar codebase from version control history and surface them as concrete questions a maintainer must answer: where is risk concentrated, who knows this code, is the project alive, does the team trust the pipeline, is anything abandoned, and is complexity load-bearing? The output is not a verdict but a structured inventory of hotspots, ownership, velocity, and firefighting frequency that other doctrine artifacts (triage, prioritisation, premortem, connascence analysis) can act on.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-forensic-repository-audit.md` |
| `TACTIC:frozen-baseline-shrink-only-ratchet` | tactic | Track the current count of a gated allowlist (call sites, dead symbols, legacy entries, or any other countable technical-debt category) in a committed baseline file. CI fails if the live count grows beyond the committed baseline, and warns (but does not fail) if it shrinks. The baseline is updated only by deliberate human action with a recorded rationale. The allowed direction is shrink-or-stay; growth is a gate failure.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-frozen-baseline-shrink-only-ratchet.md` |
| `TACTIC:glossary-curation-interview` | tactic | Systematically expand a living glossary through structured HiC-led curation rounds, ensuring all new terms are clear, well-grouped, and approved before inclusion. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-glossary-curation-interview.md` |
| `TACTIC:language-driven-design` | tactic | Treat language drift as an architectural signal. When terminology becomes inconsistent or ambiguous across code, docs, and conversation, it predicts deeper structural problems. Reviewers use linguistic checks to catch architectural issues before they manifest as bugs or coupling.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-language-driven-design.md` |
| `TACTIC:model-task-routing` | tactic | Match model strength to task difficulty: route hard-judgment work (sizing, fakeability, code-truth, review, architecture) to the strongest available model, and grounded or mechanical passes to a cheaper model. Advisory — the recommendation surfaces alongside the task, it never substitutes for the operator's or orchestrator's own judgment about who should run a step.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-model-task-routing.md` |
| `TACTIC:ownership-map-leeway` | tactic | Give implementers rationale-backed leeway to edit files adjacent to their declared owned_files surface. The hard constraint is no-overlap between work packages — not a strict prohibition on any cross-boundary edit. Strict prohibition causes workarounds (such as TODOs, deferred fixes, or duplicated logic) that are worse than the bounded out-of-map edit they prevent.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-ownership-map-leeway.md` |
| `TACTIC:paula-patterns-architecture-scout-review` | tactic | Review recurring boundary leaks, whack-a-field fixes, ownership confusion, and compatibility regressions by dispatching five architecture scouts with different lenses, then synthesizing one pragmatic matrix that separates the smallest release-safe fix from deferred architecture repair.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-paula-patterns-architecture-scout-review.md` |
| `TACTIC:pr-agent-worktree-isolation` | tactic | Govern two complementary constraints on how agents interact with PR branches: (1) agents that review or rebase a PR must execute in an isolated worktree, not in an active mission checkout; (2) scope documents must not assign patch or version numbers, because version decisions belong to the product owner at release time. Together these prevent cross-contamination of mission state and preserve the product owner's authority over the release boundary.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-pr-agent-worktree-isolation.md` |
| `TACTIC:premortem-risk-identification` | tactic | Proactively surface failure modes for a plan or decision by deliberately attempting to sabotage it before execution. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-premortem-risk-identification.md` |
| `TACTIC:problem-decomposition` | tactic | Break a complex, ambiguous problem into a set of smaller, independently tractable sub-problems before selecting a solution approach. Decomposition prevents premature convergence on a solution that addresses only part of the problem, exposes hidden scope, and creates a structured basis for work-package planning and parallel progress.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-problem-decomposition.md` |
| `TACTIC:refactoring-strangler-fig` | tactic | Replace existing functionality incrementally by running a new implementation alongside the old and rerouting behavior step by step. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-refactoring-strangler-fig.md` |
| `TACTIC:review-intent-and-risk-first` | tactic | Review work by first understanding intent and surfacing risks before suggesting changes or solutions. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-review-intent-and-risk-first.md` |
| `TACTIC:reviewer-implementer-role-separation` | tactic | Ensure that the agent or session that implements a work package is never the same agent or session that reviews it. Role separation prevents review bias, preserves the independence of the review gate, and ensures that the governing doctrine profile switches correctly between the implement and review phases.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-reviewer-implementer-role-separation.md` |
| `TACTIC:safe-to-fail-experiment` | tactic | Reframe a learning or exploration goal as a deliberately low-stakes experiment so that failure produces signal rather than shame. Running time-boxed, isolated experiments with pre-defined hypotheses accelerates skill development, surfaces assumptions early, and normalises sharing what was learned — including negative results.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-safe-to-fail-experiment.md` |
| `TACTIC:stakeholder-alignment` | tactic | Identify everyone with a meaningful stake in a decision or initiative, surface their primary concerns and success criteria, and expose tensions between groups early — before design choices embed assumptions that conflict with stakeholder reality. Unaddressed stakeholder conflict is the most common source of technically correct but organisationally rejected solutions.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-stakeholder-alignment.md` |
| `TACTIC:stopping-conditions` | tactic | Establish clear, measurable thresholds that define when to stop pursuing a goal, protecting against over-investment and sunk-cost fallacy. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-stopping-conditions.md` |
| `TACTIC:strategic-domain-classification` | tactic | Classify each bounded context as Core Domain, Supporting Subdomain, or Generic Subdomain to guide investment, staffing, and build-vs-buy decisions. Core domains receive the deepest modelling effort because they are the source of competitive advantage. Supporting subdomains are necessary but not differentiating. Generic subdomains are commodity concerns best served by off-the-shelf solutions. Based on Eric Evans's strategic classification and the Bounded Context Canvas (section 3).
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-strategic-domain-classification.md` |
| `TACTIC:tdd-red-green-refactor` | tactic | Enforce short, verifiable coding loops that improve design while keeping behavior safe. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-tdd-red-green-refactor.md` |
| `TACTIC:test-boundaries-by-responsibility` | tactic | Determine test scope by identifying which components are directly responsible for the behavior under test, rather than following structural layer boundaries. Reduces brittle tests while ensuring meaningful validation. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-test-boundaries-by-responsibility.md` |
| `TACTIC:test-minimisation` | tactic | Remove redundant tests while preserving full behavioral coverage, keeping the suite fast and easy to maintain. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-test-minimisation.md` |
| `TACTIC:test-pyramid-progression` | tactic | Run tests bottom-up through pyramid layers to get fast feedback and avoid wasting time on slow tests when fast tests fail. The execution order mirrors the ROI order: the cheapest, fastest tests run first because they catch the most bugs per second of CI time.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-test-pyramid-progression.md` |
| `TACTIC:traceable-decisions` | tactic | Ensure that material architectural and governance decisions are captured with enough context that future contributors can understand why a path was chosen and what constraints must remain true. Apply when: establishing a new pattern, choosing between alternative implementations with meaningful trade-offs, making a trade-off that accepts known costs or risks, or beginning any task with architectural implications.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-traceable-decisions.md` |
| `TACTIC:usage-examples-sync` | tactic | Keep canonical usage examples, acceptance checks, and the narrative artifacts that quote or reference them in step with behavior changes so no downstream reader is left with stale examples.
 | `_LIBRARY/tactic-usage-examples-sync.md` |
| `TACTIC:zombies-tdd` | tactic | Drive implementation through tiny behavior increments using failing tests to control complexity. | `_LIBRARY/tactic-zombies-tdd.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:adversarial-squad-cadence` | styleguide | Run a bounded multi-profile adversarial squad at each planning point-cut as strong guidance, not a gate. A mission is not blocked for skipping the squad.
 | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-adversarial-squad-cadence.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:kitty-glossary-writing` | styleguide | Clear, not clever: definitions exist to help the reader understand, not to demonstrate expertise. | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-kitty-glossary-writing.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:planning-and-tracking` | styleguide | Functional epics own work; meta-trackers only reference it. An epic must represent a real domain of work — a subsystem, a capability, or a bug-class — and own its tickets as native sub-issues. A release/stabilization/go-no-go rollup is not a domain of work: it gates via milestones or labels and references work by checklist, never as the canonical parent. Prefix such issues `META-TRACKER:` so their role is unmistakable. | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-planning-and-tracking.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:testing-principles` | styleguide | Fast: tests execute quickly enough that running them after every small change is not a burden. | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-testing-principles.md` |
| `STYLEGUIDE:tiered-standards` | styleguide | Rigour must match risk: the closer a package is to mission-critical state management or runtime execution, the higher the quality bar it must meet. | `_LIBRARY/styleguide-tiered-standards.md` |
| `TOOLGUIDE:efficient-local-tooling` | toolguide | Operation-oriented guidance for using efficient local tools during repository work. | `_LIBRARY/toolguide-efficient-local-tooling.md` |
| `TOOLGUIDE:github-tracker` | toolguide | Driving the GitHub issue tracker from the CLI — native sub-issues (parent/child), issue types, parent-chain walks, auth, and the rate-limit and node-id-vs-db-id gotchas that bite bulk tracker work.
 | `_LIBRARY/toolguide-github-tracker.md` |
| `TOOLGUIDE:terminology-guard` | toolguide | Definition unavailable in bundled doctrine. | `_LIBRARY/toolguide-terminology-guard.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:adversarial-squad-deployment` | procedure | Deploy a small, bounded set of profile-loaded subagents in parallel at high-leverage review point-cuts so independent doctrine lenses converge on findings no single reviewer would catch. Turns review from one perspective into a cheap adversarial panel that resists laziness, accidental-pass, and single-lens blind spots. Optional and charter- or memory-activated — it enriches the flow, it does not gate it.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-adversarial-squad-deployment.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:legacy-codebase-triage` | procedure | Convert an unfamiliar brownfield codebase into a defensible action plan by gathering version-control evidence, overlaying structural and complexity signals, optionally classifying domains, and bucketing the resulting findings into fix-this-week, fix-this-quarter, do-not-worry, and parallelisable work. The output is a triage document that anchors subsequent planning conversations and ADRs; it is not a replacement for deeper investigation, only a fast, evidence-backed first pass.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-legacy-codebase-triage.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:mission-tracer-files` | procedure | Give every mission a lightweight running log of tooling friction, approach evolution, and design rationale through three sparse tracer files. The files are seeded at mission start, appended to during implementation, and assessed at mission close. Captured friction and rationale feed the next mission's planning and make recurring tool and process gaps visible instead of repeatedly re-discovered.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-mission-tracer-files.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:post-merge-arch-gate-adjudication` | procedure | After merging one or more lane branches, architectural gate failures may appear that were not visible during per-lane review. This procedure distinguishes pre-existing failures (present on the mission base branch before any lane work) from regressions introduced by the merge. Correct adjudication prevents teams from either ignoring real regressions or blocking on failures they did not cause.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-post-merge-arch-gate-adjudication.md` |
| `PROCEDURE:situational-assessment` | procedure | Establish a shared, documented understanding of the context, stakeholders, constraints, and problem structure before any solution is designed or selected. A situational assessment ensures that architectural decisions are grounded in operational reality rather than technology preference, and that the trade-off assessments that follow address the right problem.
 | `_LIBRARY/procedure-situational-assessment.md` |
| `TEMPLATE_SET:software-dev-default` | template_set | Build high-quality software with structured workflows and test-driven development | `_LIBRARY/template-set-software-dev-default.md` |

## Amendment Process

Amend governance through a dedicated pull request that states the changed rule, motivation, migration impact, and affected gates. Performance threshold changes require new benchmark evidence; security or parity relaxations require explicit owner approval and an expiry or restoration plan.

## Exception Policy

Exceptions must be narrow, time-bounded, linked to a tracked issue, identify the responsible owner, preserve all unaffected gates, and include a removal criterion. No exception may permit credential exposure, unsigned updates, unauthenticated production listeners, silent loss of DSH capability, or destructive handling of user data.
